And deemest thou as those who pore, With aged eyes, short way before Emerson. 2. To pass judgment. (old) Spenser.
demonial: Of or pertaining to a demon. (old) Cudworth.
delighted: Endowed with delight. If virtue no delighted beauty lack. Shak. Syn. -- Glad; pleased; gratified. See Glad.
decomposite: 1. Compounded more than once; compounded with things already composite. 2. (Bot.) See Decompound, a., 2. | Anything decompounded. Decomposites of three metals or more. Bacon.
delirate: To madden; to rave. (old) An infatuating and delirating spirit in it. Holland.
devastavit: Waste or misapplication of the assets of a deceased person by an executor or an administrator. Bouvier.
defectibility: Deficiency; imperfection. Ld. Digby. Jer. Taylor.
dellacruscan: Of or pertaining to the Accademia della Crusca in Florence. The Dellacruscan School, a name given in satire to a class of affected English writers, most of whom lived in Florence, about a. d. 1785.
devocalize: To make toneless; to deprive of vowel quality. -- De*vo`cal*i*za"tion, n. If we take a high vowel, such as (i) [= nearly i of bit], and devocalize it, we obtain a hiss which is quite distinct enough to stand for a weak (jh). H. Sweet.
derotremata: The tribe of aquatic Amphibia which includes Amphiuma, Menopoma, etc. They have permanent gill openings, but no external gills; -- called also Cryptobranchiata. [Written also Derotrema.]
dement: To deprive of reason; to make mad. Bale. | Demented; dementate. J. H. Newman.
delicatessen: Relishes for the table; dainties; delicacies. "A dealer in delicatessen". G. H. Putnam.
deblai: The cavity from which the earth for parapets, etc. (remblai), is taken.
defunct: Having finished the course of life; dead; deceased. "Defunct organs." Shak. The boar, defunct, lay tripped up, near. Byron.
desegmentation: The loss or obliteration of division into segments; as, a desegmentation of the body.
dementia: Insanity; madness; esp. that form which consists in weakness or total loss of thought and reason; mental imbecility; idiocy.
despicably: In a despicable or mean manner; contemptibly; as, despicably stingy.
deferent: Serving to carry; bearing. "Bodies deferent." Bacon. | 1. That which carries or conveys. Though air be the most favorable deferent of sounds. Bacon. 2. (Ptolemaic Astron.) An imaginary circle surrounding the earth, in whose periphery either the heavenly…
decennoval: Pertaining to the number nineteen; of nineteen years. Holder.
decacerata: The division of Cephalopoda which includes the squids, cuttlefishes, and others having ten arms or tentacles; -- called also Decapoda. [Written also Decacera.] See Dibranchiata.
decitizenize: To deprive of the rights of citizenship. We have no law -- as the French have -- to decitizenize a citizen. Edw. Bates.
deprehend: 1. To take unwares or by surprise; to seize, as a person commiting an unlawful act; to catch; to apprehend. The deprehended adulteress.Jer. Taylor. 2. To detect; to discover; to find out. The motion . . . are to be deprehended by experience. Bacon.
defendant: 1. Serving, or suitable, for defense; defensive. (old) With men of courage and with means defendant. Shak. 2. Making defense. | 1. One who defends; a defender. The rampiers and ditches which the defendants had cast up. Spotswood. 2. (Law) A person required to make answer in an action or suit; -- opposed to plaintiff. Abbott.
dehort: To urge to abstain or refrain; to dissuade. (old) The apostles vehemently dehort us from unbelief. Bp. Ward. "Exhort" remains, but dehort, a word whose place neither "dissuade" nor any other exactly supplies, has escaped us. Trench.
demogorgon: , A mysterious, terrible, and evil divinity, regarded by some as the author of creation, by others as a great magician who was supposed to command the spirits of the lower world. See Gorgon. Orcus and Ades, and the dreaded name Of Demogorgon. Milton.
delirifacient: Producing, or tending to produce, delirium. -- n. Any substance which tends to cause delirium.
dentirostral: Having a toothed bill; -- applied to a group of passerine birds, having the bill notched, and feeding chiefly on insects, as the shrikes and vireos. See Illust. (N) under Beak.
decastere: A measure of capacity, equal to ten steres, or ten cubic meters.
dextronic: Pertaining to, or derived from, dextrose; as, dextronic acid. Dextronic acid, a sirupy substance obtained by the partial oxidation of various carbohydrates, as dextrose, etc.
defile: To march off in a line, file by file; to file off. | 1. Any narrow passage or gorge in which troops can march only in a file, or with a narrow front; a long, narrow pass between hills, rocks, etc. 2. (Mil.) The act of defilading a fortress, or of…
decrepitude: The broken state produced by decay and the infirmities of age; infirm old age.
depositor: One who makes a deposit, especially of money in bank; -- the correlative of depository.
decant: To pour off gently, as liquor, so as not to disturb the sediment; or to pour from one vessel into another; as, to decant wine.
decadal: Pertaining to ten; consisting of tens.
decile: An aspect or position of two planets, when they are distant from each other a tenth part of the zodiac, or 36º.
demilune: 1. (Fort.) A work constructed beyond the main ditch of a fortress, and in front of the curtain between two bastions, intended to defend the curtain; a ravelin. See Ravelin. 2. (Physiol.) A crescentic mass of granular protoplasm present in the salivary glands.
deordination: Disorder; dissoluteness. (old) Excess of rideordination. Jer. Taylor.
delphic: 1. Of or relating to Delphi, or to the famous oracle of that place. 2. Ambiguous; mysterious. "If he is silent or delphic." New York Times.
dentilingual: Produced by applying the tongue to the teeth or to the gums; or representing a sound so formed. -- n. A dentilingual sound or letter. The letters of this fourth, dentilingual or linguidental, class, viz., d, t, s, z, l, r. Am. Cyc.
deculassement: An accidental blowing off of, or other serious damage to, the breechblock of a gun; also, a removal of the breechblock for the purpose of disabling the gun.
deluder: One who deludes; a deceiver; an impostor.
devilfish: (a) A huge ray (Manta birostris or Cephaloptera vampyrus) of the Gulf of Mexico and Southern Atlantic coasts. Several other related species take the same name. See Cephaloptera. (b) A large cephalopod, especially the very large species of Octopus and Architeuthis. See Octopus. (c) The gray whale of the Pacific coast. See Gray whale.
deltoid: Shaped like the Greek Deltoid leaf (Bot.), a leaf in the form of a triangle with the stem inserted at the middle of the base. -- Deltoid muscle (Anat.), a triangular muscle in the shoulder which serves to move the arm directly upward.
desquamation: The separation or shedding of the cuticle or epidermis in the form of flakes or scales; exfoliation, as of bones.
destructible: Liable to destruction; capable of being destroyed.
demoniacism: The state of being demoniac, or the practices of demoniacs.
decennovary: Pertaining to the number nineteen; of nineteen years. Holder.
dehydrate: To deprive of water; to render free from water; as, to dehydrate alcohol.
desiccator: 1. One who, or that which, desiccates. 2. (Chem.) A short glass jar fitted with an air-tight cover, and containing some desiccating agent, as sulphuric acid or calcium chloride, above which is suspended the material to be dried, or preserved from moisture.
desolater: One who, or that which, desolates or lays waste. Mede.
detrital: Pertaining to, or composed of, detritus.
descry: 1. To spy out or discover by the eye, as objects distant or obscure; to espy; to recognize; to discern; to discover. And the house of Joseph sent to descry Bethel. Judg. i. 23. | , Discovery or view, as of an army seen at a distance. (old) Near, and on speedy foot; the main descry Stands on the hourly thought. Shak.
destroy: 1. To unbuild; to pull or tear down; to separate virulently into its constituent parts; to break up the structure and organic existence of; to demolish. But ye shall destroy their altars, break their images, and cut down their groves. Ex. xxxiv. 13. 2. To ruin; to bring to naught; to put an end to; to annihilate; to consume. I will utterly pluck up and destroy that nation.
decrescent: Becoming less by gradual diminution; decreasing; as, a decrescent moon. | A crescent with the horns directed towards the sinister. Cussans.
debut: A beginning or first attempt; hence, a first appearance before the public, as of an actor or public speaker.
demonology: A treatise on demons; a supposititious science which treats of demons and their manifestations. Sir W. Scott.
destroyer: One who destroys, ruins, kills, or desolates.
dexterous: 1. Ready and expert in the use of the body and limbs; skillful and active with the hands; handy; ready; as, a dexterous hand; a dexterous workman. 2. Skillful in contrivance; quick at inventing expedients; expert; as, a dexterous manager. Dexterous the craving, fawning crowd to quit. Pope. 3. Done with dexterity; skillful; artful; as, dexterous management.
dernful: Secret; hence, lonely; sad; mournful. (old) "Dernful noise." Spenser.
delirament: A wandering of the mind; a crazy fancy. (old) Heywood.
demigorge: Half the gorge, or entrance into a bastion, taken from the angle of the flank to the center of the bastion.
detur: A present of books given to a meritorious undergraduate student as a prize. [Harvard Univ., U. S.]
desire: 1. To long for; to wish for earnestly; to covet. Neither shall any man desire thy land. Ex. xxxiv. 24. Ye desire your child to live. Tennyson. 2. To express a wish for; to entreat; to request. | 1. The natural longing that is excited by the enjoyment or the thought of any good, and impels to action or effort its continuance or possession; an eager wish to obtain or enjoy.
despond: To give up, the will, courage, or spirit; to be thoroughly disheartened; to lose all courage; to become dispirited or depressed; to take an unhopeful view. I should despair, or at least despond. | Despondency. (old) The slough of despond. Bunyan.
decreaseless: Suffering no decrease. It [the river] flows and flows, and yet will flow, Volume decreaseless to the final hour. A. Seward.
debellate: To subdue; to conquer in war. (old) Speed.
deftness: The quality of being deft. Drayton.
defective: 1. Wanting in something; incomplete; lacking a part; deficient; imperfect; faulty; -- applied either to natural or moral qualities; as, a defective limb; defective timber; a defective copy or account; a defective character; defective rules. 2. (Gram.) Lacking some of the usual forms of declension or conjugation; as, a defective noun or verb. -- De*fect"ive*ly, adv.
decumbent: 1. Lying down; prostrate; recumbent. The decumbent portraiture of a woman. Ashmole. 2. (Bot.) Reclining on the ground, as if too weak to stand, and tending to rise at the summit or apex; as, a decumbent stem. Gray.
decrease: To grow less, -- opposed to increase; to be diminished gradually, in size, degree, number, duration, etc., or in strength, quality, or excellence; as, they days decrease in length from June to… | To cause to grow less; to diminish gradually; as, extravagance decreases one's means. That might decrease their present store. Prior.
depletive: Able or fitted to deplete. -- n. A substance used to deplete.
devilize: To make a devil of. He that should deify a saint, should wrong him as much as he that should devilize him. Bp. Hall.
deponent: 1. (Law) One who deposes or testifies under oath; one who gives evidence; usually, one who testifies in writing. 2. (Gr. & Lat. Gram.) A deponent verb. Syn. -- Deponent, Affiant. | Having a passive form with an active meaning, as certain latin and Greek verbs.
demonist: A believer in, or worshiper of, demons.
decani: Used of the side of the choir on which the dean's stall is placed; decanal; -- correlative to cantoris; as, the decanal, or decani, side.
defensible: 1. Capable of being defended; as, a defensible city, or a defensible cause. 2. Capable of offering defense. (old) Shak.
devotionality: The practice of a devotionalist. A. H. Clough.
desirefulness: The state of being desireful; eagerness to obtain and possess. The desirefulness of our minds much augmenteth and increaseth our pleasure. Udall.
defacer: One who, or that which, defaces or disfigures.
decil: An aspect or position of two planets, when they are distant from each other a tenth part of the zodiac, or 36º.
decayed: Fallen, as to physical or social condition; affected with decay; rotten; as, decayed vegetation or vegetables; a decayed fortune or gentleman. -- De*cay"ed*ness, n.
deltaconnection: One of the usual forms or methods for connecting apparatus to a three-phase circuit, the three corners of the delta or triangle, as diagrammatically represented, being connected to the three wires of the supply circuit.
demotics: The department of knowledge relative to the care and culture of the people; sociology in its broadest sense; -- in library cataloguing.
decapoda: 1. (Zoöl.) The order of Crustacea which includes the shrimps, lobsters, crabs, etc. Note: They have a carapace, covering and uniting the somites of the head and thorax and inclosing a gill chamber on each side, and usually have five (rarely six) pairs of legs. They are divided into two principal groups: Brachyura and Macrura.
defensative: That which serves to protect or defend.
dealfish: A long, thin fish of the arctic seas (Trachypterus arcticus).
death: 1. The cessation of all vital phenomena without capability of resuscitation, either in animals or plants. Note: Local death is going on at times and in all parts of the living body, in which individual cells and elements are being cast off and replaced by new; a process essential to life. General death is of two kinds;
devildiver: A small water bird. See Dabchick.
deducible: 1. Capable of being deduced or inferred; derivable by reasoning, as a result or consequence. All properties of a triangle depend on, and are deducible from, the complex idea of three lines including a space. Locke. 2. Capable of being brought down. (old) As if God [were] deducible to human imbecility. State Trials (1649).
dermis: The deep sensitive layer of the skin beneath the scarfskin or epidermis; -- called also true skin, derm, derma, corium, cutis, and enderon. See Skin, and Illust. in Appendix.
detruncate: To shorten by cutting; to cut off; to lop off.
dendroidal: Resembling a shrub or tree in form; treelike.
declinometer: An instrument for measuring the declination of the magnetic needle.
dentate: 1. (Bot.) Toothed; especially, with the teeth projecting straight out, not pointed either forward or backward; as, a dentate leaf. 2. (Zoöl.) Having teeth or toothlike points. See Illust. of Antennæ.
depulsory: Driving or thrusting away; averting. Holland.
deflector: That which deflects, as a diaphragm in a furnace, or a come in a lamp (to deflect and mingle air and gases and help combustion).
deductive: Of or pertaining to deduction; capable of being deduced from premises; deducible. All knowledge of causes is deductive. Glanvill. Notions and ideas . . . used in a deductive process. Whewell.
deutoplasm: The lifeless food matter in the cytoplasm of an ovum or a cell, as distinguished from the active or true protoplasm; yolk substance; yolk.
debruised: Surmounted by an ordinary; as, a lion is debruised when a bend or other ordinary is placed over it, as in the cut. The lion of England and the lilies of France without the baton sinister, under which, according to the laws of heraldry, they where debruised in token of his illegitimate birth. Macaulay.
depauperate: To make poor; to impoverish. Liming does not depauperate; the ground will last long, and bear large grain. Mortimer. Humility of mind which depauperates the spirit. Jer. Taylor. | Falling short of the natural size, from being impoverished or starved. Gray.
detract: 1. To take away; to withdraw. Detract much from the view of the without. Sir H. Wotton. 2. To take credit or reputation from; to defame. That calumnious critic . . . | To take away a part or something, especially from one's credit; to lessen reputation; to derogate; to defame; -- often with from. It has been the fashion to detract both from the moral and literary…
detestableness: The quality or state of being detestable.
derange: 1. To put out of place, order, or rank; to disturb the proper arrangement or order of; to throw into disorder, confusion, or embarrassment; to disorder; to disarrange; as, to derange the plans of a commander, or the affairs of a nation. 2. To disturb in action or function, as a part or organ, or the whole of a machine or organism.
delthyris: A name formerly given to certain Silurian brachiopod shells of the genus Spirifer. Delthyris limestone (Geol.), one of the divisions of the Upper Silurian rocks in New York.
dentiloquy: The habit or practice of speaking through the teeth, or with them closed.
delilah: The mistress of Samson, who betrayed him (Judges xvi.); hence, a harlot; a temptress. Other Delilahs on a smaller scale Burns met with during his Dumfries sojourn. J. C. Shairp.
deutzia: A genus of shrubs with pretty white flowers, much cultivated.
deposable: Capable of being deposed or deprived of office. Howell.
derrick: A mast, spar, or tall frame, supported at the top by stays or guys, with suitable tackle for hoisting heavy weights, as stones in building. Derrick crane, a combination of the derrick and the crane, having facility for hoisting and also for swinging the load horizontally.
deference: A yielding of judgment or preference from respect to the wishes or opinion of another; submission in opinion; regard; respect; complaisance. Deference to the authority of thoughtful and sagacious men. Whewell. Deference is the most complicate, the most indirect, and the most elegant of all compliments. Shenstone. Syn. -- Deference, Reverence, Respect.
denticete: The division of Cetacea in which the teeth are developed, including the sperm whale, dolphins, etc.
decurrent: Extending downward; -- said of a leaf whose base extends downward and forms a wing along the stem. -- De*cur"rent*ly, adv.
deign: 1. To esteem worthy; to consider worth notice; -- opposed to disdain. (old) I fear my Julia would not deign my lines. Shak. 2. To condescend to give or bestow; to stoop to furnish; to vouchsafe; | To think worthy; to vouchsafe; to condescend; -- followed by an infinitive. O deign to visit our forsaken seats. Pope. Yet not Lord Cranstone deigned she greet. Sir W. Scott.
decidement: Means of forming a decision. (old) Beau. & Fl.
deprive: 1. To take away; to put an end; to destroy. (old) 'Tis honor to deprive dishonored life. Shak. 2. To dispossess; to bereave; to divest; to hinder from possessing; to debar; to shut out from; -- with a remoter object, usually preceded by of. God hath deprived her of wisdom. Job xxxix. 17. It was seldom that anger deprived him of power over himself. Macaulay. 3.
deletery: Destructive; poisonous. (old) "Deletery medicines." Hudibras. | That which destroys. (old) They [the Scriptures] are the only deletery of heresies. Jer. Taylor.
derivable: That can be derived; obtainable by transmission; capable of being known by inference, as from premises or data; capable of being traced, as from a radical; as, income is derivable from various sources. All honor derivable upon me. South. The exquisite pleasure derivable from the true and beautiful relations of domestic life. H. G. Bell.
demiurge: 1. (Gr. Antiq.) The chief magistrate in some of the Greek states. 2. God, as the Maker of the world. 3. According to the Gnostics, an agent or one employed by the Supreme Being to create the material universe and man.
despotical: Having the character of, or pertaining to, a despot; absolute in power; possessing and abusing unlimited power; evincing despotism; tyrannical; arbitrary. -- Des*pot"ic*al*ly, adv. -- Des*pot"ic*al*ness, n.
dehorn: To deprive of horns; to prevent the growth or the horns of (cattle) by burning their ends soon after they start. See Dishorn. "Dehorning cattle." Farm Journal (1886).
deuce: 1. (Gaming) Two; a card or a die with two spots; as, the deuce of hearts. 2. (Tennis) A condition of the score beginning whendeuce, which decides the game. | The devil; a demon. [A euphemism, written also deuse.] [Low]
decursively: In a decursive manner. Decursively pinnate (Bot.), having the leaflets decurrent, or running along the petiole; -- said of a leaf.
dedimus: A writ to commission private persons to do some act in place of a judge, as to examine a witness, etc. Bouvier.
deathful: 1. Full of death or slaughter; murderous; destructive; bloody. These eyes behold The deathful scene. Pope. 2. Liable to undergo death; mortal. The deathless gods and deathful earth. Chapman.
deferment: The act of delaying; postponement. My grief, joined with the instant business, Begs a deferment. Suckling.
debosh: To debauch. (old) "A deboshed lady." Beau. & Fl.
decapitate: 1. To cut off the head of; to behead. 2. To remove summarily from office. [Colloq. U. S.]
declinator: 1. An instrument for taking the declination or angle which a plane makes with the horizontal plane. 2. A dissentient. Bp. Hacket.
dermal: 1. Pertaining to the integument or skin of animals; dermic; as, the dermal secretions. 2. (Anat.) Pertaining to the dermis or true skin.
decolletage: The upper border or part of a décolleté corsage.
democratical: Democratic. The democratical was democratically received. Algernon Sidney.
debarb: To deprive of the beard. (old) Bailey.
deltaic: Relating to, or like, a delta.
developable: Capable of being developed. J. Peile. Developable surface (Math.), a surface described by a moving right line, and such that consecutive positions of the generator intersect each other. Hence, the surface can be developed into a plane.
deepen: 1. To make deep or deeper; to increase the depth of; to sink lower; as, to deepen a well or a channel. It would . . . deepen the bed of the Tiber. Addison. 2. To make darker or more intense; | To become deeper; as, the water deepens at every cast of the lead; the plot deepens. His blood-red tresses deepening in the sun. Byron.
denigrate: 1. To blacken thoroughly; to make very black. Boyle. 2. Fig.: To blacken or sully; to defame. To denigrate the memory of Voltaire. Morley.
decrepitate: To roast or calcine so as to cause a crackling noise; as, to decrepitate salt. | To crackle, as salt in roasting.
debatement: Controversy; deliberation; debate. A serious question and debatement with myself. Milton.
declare: 1. To make clear; to free from obscurity. (old) "To declare this a little." Boyle. 2. To make known by language; to communicate or manifest explicitly and plainly in any way; to exhibit; to publish; | 1. To make a declaration, or an open and explicit avowal; to proclaim one's self; -- often with for or against; as, victory declares against the allies. Like fawning courtiers, for success they wait,…
depatriate: To withdraw, or cause to withdraw, from one's country; to banish. (old) A subject born in any state May, if he please, depatriate. Mason.
despair: To be hopeless; to have no hope; to give up all hope or expectation; -- often with of. We despaired even of life. 2 Cor. i. 8. Never despair of God's blessings here. Wake. Syn. -- See Despond. | 1. To give up as beyond hope or expectation; to despair of. (old) I would not despair the greatest design that could be attempted. Milton. 2. To cause to despair. (old) Sir W. Williams.
decorator: One who decorates, adorns, or embellishes; specifically, an artisan whose business is the decoration of houses, esp. their interior decoration.
deltidium: The triangular space under the beak of many brachiopod shells.
despecificate: To discriminate; to separate according to specific signification or qualities; to specificate; to desynonymize. Inaptitude and ineptitude have been usefully despecificated. Fitzed. Hall.
demarcation: The act of marking, or of ascertaining and setting a limit; separation; distinction. The speculative line of demarcation, where obedience ought to end and resistance must begin, is faint, obscure, and not easily definable. Burke.
deoxygenation: The act or operation of depriving of oxygen.
demountable: Capable of being dismounted; -- said of a form of rim, for an automobile wheel, which can be removed with its tire from the wheel.
dezincification: The act or process of freeing from zinc; also, the condition resulting from the removal of zinc.
deletive: Adapted to destroy or obliterate. Evelyn.
defoliation: The separation of ripened leaves from a branch or stem; the falling or shedding of the leaves.
